about.title: About Me
about.experienceText: I build web applications with React and TypeScript. I have worked on data-heavy platforms — real estate valuation systems used by Turkish banks, and Land Registry projects. My own products in Vue and React Native I take end to end.
about.beyondText: I do not stop at the client. I write the API endpoints, validation and security rules my own features need. The contact form on this site is a small example: a shared Zod schema, rate limiting and Turnstile.
about.howIWorkText: I build code quality into the process rather than leaving it to intent. Small, focused pull requests, a commit history that explains itself, and a CI pipeline that lets nothing broken through. This site was built that way.
about.goalsText: Rather than switching technologies I go deeper into the ones I use. Lately that means TypeScript's type system, performance work, and moving quickly through a codebase somebody else wrote.

vargeloglu-insaat.title: Bringing a dead corporate site back online
vargeloglu-insaat.summary: Vargeloğlu İnşaat's website had gone offline and nobody could reach the server it lived on. Getting back in came first; rebuilding came second.
vargeloglu-insaat.role: Sole developer — recovery, rebuild, content, deployment, SEO
vargeloglu-insaat.stack: Vue 3 · TypeScript · Composition API · Vercel · Cloudflare
vargeloglu-insaat.timeline: Three weeks of build, on top of a longer recovery
vargeloglu-insaat.metricsHeading: Three months of Search Console data

sections.heading: The problem
body: Vargeloğlu İnşaat is a construction company that gets most of its work through the jobs it has already finished. One project leads to a recommendation, that leads to the next. The website is there to reach the people who are not already in that circle.
Their old site had stopped loading. The hosting had expired, the SSL certificate along with it, and the site had been down long enough that nobody was quite sure what was still recoverable.
The client owned the domain. He did not have the hosting login, and the content — years of project photographs, the reference list, all the copy — was sitting on a server neither of us could open.

sections.heading: Getting the content back
body: This part took longer than writing the site. I spent several days going back and forth with the hosting company by phone and email until they restored control panel access.
Once I was in, I pulled out everything that was worth keeping before anything else lapsed: the copy, the project photographs, the reference list. Only after that could we talk about what to build.

sections.heading: The rebuild
body: I built it in Vue 3 with the Composition API. React is what I use professionally, and I picked Vue here deliberately: this was a project I owned end to end, the deadline was mine, and the requirements — a content site with a gallery and a way to get in touch — did not push toward one framework over the other. I wanted to learn a second ecosystem on a real project rather than a tutorial. It slowed me down for the first few days and left me able to read Vue code properly.
The build took about three weeks. Most of it landed in the first ten days; the rest was refinement.

items.text: Turkish and English, because the company works with contractors who do not all read Turkish. The chosen language is saved and applied to the lang attribute when the page loads, so returning visitors land where they left off and screen readers pronounce the page correctly.

Split across four categories: infrastructure and drainage, site and road concrete, stone walling, landscaping. The lightbox was the easy part. Construction photographs do not explain themselves — the same pile of earth is excavation to one person and demolition to another. Working out what the categories should be, then going through 187 images one by one, took longer than writing the component.

items.term: Content I wrote, not content I copied.
items.text: Some text came across from the old site. Most of it I drafted and the client approved. The numbers on the homepage — years in business, completed projects, references — came from him, because the ones on the old site were years stale.
I wrote a brief, generated a set of logo candidates with AI, picked one and cleaned it up for production. Where the client had no photograph for something, I found and prepared one.

items.term: Performance during the build, not after.
items.text: The hero slider and intro imagery were converted to WebP while I was working on them, rather than in a cleanup pass once someone complained about load times.
Local search traffic for a business like this arrives almost entirely on phones.

sections.heading: The migration nobody sees
body: Replacing a site Google already knows is a different job from launching a new one. The old WordPress URLs were still sitting in the index, and every one of them now pointed at nothing.

I moved DNS to Cloudflare and deployment to Vercel. Propagation took about a day worldwide. There was no downtime to plan around, since the old site had already been unreachable for a while — the switch could only be an improvement.

Search Console showed the rest: pages Google refused to index, crawl errors left over from the old structure, and the wait while a new sitemap was accepted. I set up Analytics at the same time so the client could watch the traffic himself instead of taking my word for it.

sections.heading: Results
body: The absolute numbers are small, and for a local construction firm they should be — the search volume is what it is. Position and click-through rate are the ones I look at.

Sitting near the top of the first page means the ranking the old domain had built up came across instead of being lost, which is the usual way these migrations go wrong. A 15.2% click-through rate is well above average, which tells me the titles and descriptions are pulling their weight.
On the company's own name — the query that matters most — the site gets 22 clicks from 51 impressions. People looking for this business find it.
PageSpeed Insights on mobile: SEO 100, best practices 100, accessibility 84, performance 69.

sections.heading: What I have not finished
body: I check this site rather than assume it is fine, and the numbers say the migration is not done.

items.term: The old URLs are still indexed.
items.text: Three legacy paths pulled 112 impressions over three months and produced 3 clicks between them. They still rank; they just go nowhere. The deployment config redirects the apex domain to www and does nothing else, so the ranking those pages still carry is leaking away instead of moving to the new ones. Adding 301s from the old structure is the next thing I do.

items.term: Two of nine pages are indexed.
items.text: Five are excluded as “alternate page with proper canonical tag”. That is what a single-page app looks like when it serves one static canonical tag: every route claims to be the home page and Google files the rest as duplicates. One more returns a 5xx. I ran into exactly this on this portfolio and fixed it by deriving canonical and hreflang per route.
Lower than a content site should be. The images are already WebP, so the groundwork is there, but image delivery and render-blocking resources have not had the pass this portfolio got.
The deployment config sets no CSP, HSTS or X-Content-Type-Options. Not urgent for a brochure site whose only input is a contact form, but it is on the list.

portfolio.title: Rebuilding the portfolio I started in 2023
portfolio.summary: I set this site up in July 2023, barely touched it for two and a half years, and came back to find every shortcut still sitting where I left it. The git history reads like a record of what I did not know yet.
portfolio.role: Everything — architecture, build tooling, backend, CI, content
portfolio.stack: React 18 · TypeScript · Vite · Vercel Functions · Firebase · Cloudflare
portfolio.timeline: Created July 2023 · revived December 2025 · rebuilt August 2026

sections.heading: What the git log records
body: The history splits into three eras, and the commit messages give each one away.
July 2023: six commits, named v3, v4, v5 and “firts portfolio commit”. Create React App, a dark theme, five sections. Then nothing for two and a half years while I was busy with client work.

December 2025 through July 2026: about fifty commits. This is where I started caring — Firebase visitor tracking, Turkish and English content, Search Console, structured data, a sitemap. Pull requests appear for the first time around April. The messages get better too, though CI=false build for vercel and two commits called test are still in there.
August 2026: seventy-four commits, more than half the project's history, done in two weeks. That is the rebuild this page is about.

sections.heading: What I found when I came back
body: Coming back to your own old code after three years is a useful exercise. You are far enough away to read it like a stranger, but you cannot blame anyone else.

The projects page shipped a 2.2 MB PNG. Project cards hid their titles and buttons behind :hover, which on a phone meant two grey rectangles and nothing else. There was no router, so every URL rendered the home page — including the ones that should have been 404s. The single test in the suite was the create-react-app default, and it failed.

There was also a CI=false flag in the build script, put there at some point to stop warnings from failing the build. When I removed it, the build was clean. It had been guarding against nothing for months.

sections.heading: Working in phases
body: I split the rebuild into four phases and gave each one a pull request. Hygiene, then the mobile and accessibility failures, then build tooling and routing, then infrastructure. Nothing reached master without passing CI.
The order mattered. Fixing the hover bug before there was a router would have meant touching the same components twice. Adding TypeScript before the Vite migration would have meant migrating twice.

items.text: English at the root, Turkish under /tr. Both are separately indexable, a shared link keeps its language, and the lang attribute comes from the route. Slugs live in one JSON file that the router, the navbar and the sitemap generator all read, so those three cannot drift apart.

As a single-page app the site carried one canonical tag in index.html, so every route told Google it was the home page. Nine of ten routes were effectively invisible. Canonical, og:url and hreflang now come from the route, confirmed through Search Console's live test.

Full-resolution PNGs live outside the bundle. A sharp pipeline crops project screenshots to a shared 2:1 ratio, sizes everything at twice its display width, and writes WebP. 3.73 MB of sources become 233 KB of output.

items.term: Vite's asset inlining had to be switched off.
items.text: It base64-inlines anything under 4 kB, which caught most of the icons and pushed the bundle from 104 to 140 kB gzip. Base64 adds a third to the size and compresses badly. The same trap had been costing me bytes under create-react-app, with PNGs, without my noticing.

items.term: The contact form is mine end to end.
items.text: It used to POST to a third-party endpoint and navigate the visitor away with no confirmation. Now a Vercel function validates with a Zod schema shared with the form, checks a honeypot, rate limits per IP, verifies a Cloudflare Turnstile token, and sends through Resend from my own domain. The client validates too, but only for fast feedback — the server is the gate.

items.term: The visitor counter, properly this time.
items.text: I had noticed the race condition back in May and committed a partial fix. It was still a read followed by a write, so two people arriving together still cancelled each other out. This time it is a transaction, deduplication moved from localStorage to a server-side claim that can be created but never updated, and a security rule accepts nothing but serverTimestamp() for presence.

sections.heading: What CI actually guards
body: Every pull request runs typecheck, lint, tests and build, and master is protected so none of it can be skipped. A separate job runs Lighthouse against three routes.

Calibrating it was the interesting part. A pull request that changed one CSS class failed with a performance score of 0.66, then passed at 100 on a re-run — shared runners throttle, and every time-based metric moves with them. An alarm that fires at random teaches you to press re-run instead of investigate.

So performance became a warning, and the blocking assertions moved to things CPU contention cannot touch: total byte weight under 600 kB, modern image formats, minification. Those catch the regression I actually worry about, which is a large unoptimised image finding its way back in.

sections.heading: Two bugs that only appeared in production
body: The visitor stats spun forever on desktop while working fine on mobile. Firebase falls back to long polling when WebSocket is blocked, and that transport works by injecting a script tag — which my own Content Security Policy blocked. One CSP directive fixed it. The more useful lesson was underneath: the failed read had no error handler, so the loading state never cleared. It now renders nothing rather than a wrong number.

The contact form locked itself after five minutes. Turnstile tokens expire, and I had wired the expiry callback to the same handler as the error callback, so a routine part of the token lifecycle was being treated as a broken widget.

sections.heading: What is next
body: Case studies for the remaining projects, and a tighter performance budget as more content lands here. The dependency audit is reviewed rather than silenced: five advisories remain, all inside the Lighthouse CI toolchain, and the README explains why dropping to a 2020 release to clear them would be the wrong trade.

gaming-pro-market.title: Building an e-commerce platform with a team of seven
gaming-pro-market.summary: A full storefront and admin panel, built by seven people over three and a half months. My share was the auth flow, the cart, user addresses and most of the admin user management. The backend it talked to is long gone, so this is a look at the code rather than the site.
gaming-pro-market.role: Frontend developer — auth, cart, addresses, admin user management, API layer
gaming-pro-market.stack: React 18 · Redux Toolkit · React Router 6 · Formik · Yup · SCSS · Bootstrap
gaming-pro-market.statusNote: The repository is private and the Heroku backend it depended on no longer runs, so there is no code or live link to offer here. Everything below is written from the source I still have locally.

sections.heading: How the team worked
body: Seven of us, though four did most of the work. We picked a team lead and split the application into modules by agreement rather than assignment — someone would take the shop pages, someone the checkout flow, and so on.

I took the authentication screens, the cart, user addresses, and most of the admin user management: listing users and editing a single user's addresses, coupons, orders and reviews. I also wrote a good part of the API service layer that everything else called into.

items.text: Login, registration, forgot password and reset password, including the email confirmation step. Formik and Yup handled the forms; the token went into encrypted storage and the session was restored on app start so a refresh did not log you out.
A Redux slice backed by the server, with add, increment, decrement and remove all synchronised against the API rather than kept only in local state.
The area I spent the most time in. Straightforward CRUD, but it touches checkout, admin and the profile page at once, so the shape of the data had to work in three places.
A user list plus a per-user edit screen with tabs for that user's addresses, coupons, orders and reviews — four separate resources joined by one identifier.
Product, order, review, coupon, address and contact services. One module per resource, each wrapping axios and attaching the auth header.

sections.heading: What I would do differently
body: Going back through this code with what I know now, five things stand out. None of them are anyone's mistake in particular — they are the decisions a team makes when it is learning.

items.term: The storage encryption key shipped to the browser.
items.text: We stored the auth token with encrypt-storage, and the key came from an environment variable prefixed REACT_APP_ — which means the build compiled it straight into the bundle. Anyone who could read the encrypted token could read the key beside it. The decision was made in good faith, but the threat model was missing: the attack it was meant to stop is XSS, and against XSS the only real answer is an httpOnly cookie the page cannot read at all.

Every admin route was individually wrapped in a ProtectedRoute element. React Router 6 has layout routes for exactly this: one wrapper around a group. Thirty repetitions is thirty chances to forget one when adding a page, which is the kind of gap that only shows up after it matters.

Every page was imported eagerly at the top of the router file, so an anonymous visitor browsing products downloaded the entire admin panel — product editing, coupon assignment, reports. Lazy routes would have cut the first load substantially.

items.term: The router and the routes lived in the same file.
items.text: BrowserRouter was created in the middle of the route definitions, which makes the routes untestable — you cannot wrap them in a MemoryRouter to assert on navigation. Separating the two is one line and it unlocks the whole category of routing tests.

Two bugs came from the same root. Decrementing allowed the quantity to reach zero, leaving items sitting in the cart with a count of nothing. And the add action looked for an existing item by payload.id while every other part of the cart keyed on productId, so the same product could be added twice as separate rows. A single validated shape for a cart item, applied on every path that writes to it, would have removed both.

sections.heading: What it was worth
body: This was the first time I worked in a team where the pieces had to fit together without anyone holding the whole picture. Merge conflicts, agreeing on the shape of an API response before either side existed, working out whose module a bug belonged to — none of that is visible in the code, and all of it was the point.

The habits I keep from it are mostly about interfaces: agree on the data shape early, keep one module per resource, and make the boundary between your area and someone else's explicit. The habits I have added since are the ones this project did not have — types, tests, and a pipeline that says no.
